fragments.subject: station
fragments.text: This looks like a ward station: a long wooden counter with shelves behind it, where staff kept records and watched the corridor.

fragments.subject: station
fragments.text: The station looks lived-in again: a green desk lamp, a bound day book and a brass call bell on the counter, and a chair pulled up behind it. If this were 1953, I'd guess someone was on night duty here, with the lamp turned toward the hall.

fragments.subject: station
fragments.text: There's a small round spot near the right end of the counter, cleaner than the wood around it.

fragments.subject: station
fragments.text: In the middle of the counter the dust leaves a clean rectangle, about the size of a ledger.

fragments.subject: station
fragments.text: A wooden chair lies on its back behind the counter.

fragments.subject: station
fragments.text: Kirkbride's ward plan called for an attendant's room on every ward, close enough to keep watch over the patients at night.

fragments.subject: station
fragments.text: Night staff often kept a lamp burning at the station, so anyone who woke up frightened could see that someone was there.

fragments.subject: station
fragments.text: Desk lamps like that were often carried off or knocked aside by scrappers. If it's still on this ward, it may be lying in one of the rooms off the corridor.

fragments.subject: station
fragments.text: Wards usually kept a day book at the station: a running record of meals, moods and visitors, written up shift by shift.

fragments.subject: station
fragments.text: Things on a ward tended to travel the routes staff used every day. The dining room and its dumbwaiter would have been one of them.

fragments.subject: station
fragments.text: Many stations kept a small call bell on the counter, so a patient could summon staff without raising her voice.

fragments.subject: station
fragments.text: A bell is small and easy to kick into a corner. It could be in any of the rooms along the north side.

fragments.subject: station
fragments.text: One more thing. There seems to be someone standing behind the counter in your photo, a woman in white with a small cap. Is this a recent picture? As far as I know, this building has been closed since 1989.

fragments.subject: piano
fragments.text: This looks like an upright piano, probably a hundred years old or more. The case is water-stained and the music shelf is empty.

fragments.subject: piano
fragments.text: Pianos were common in asylum day rooms of this era. The Kirkbride approach held that comfortable, home-like surroundings helped patients recover, and music and gatherings were part of that idea.

fragments.subject: piano
fragments.text: There's a clean rectangle in the dust on top, as if a book sat there for a long time.

fragments.subject: piano_plate
fragments.text: A small brass maker's plate. Most of the lettering has worn away, but I can make out "GRAND RAPIDS, MICH." and part of a serial number.

fragments.subject: piano_plate
fragments.text: Grand Rapids was known as Furniture City around the turn of the last century, so a piano from there would fit a Michigan state hospital buying close to home.

fragments.subject: bay_window
fragments.text: Tall windows with old wavy glass, set in a bay that looks out toward the water.

fragments.subject: bay_window
fragments.text: Building 50 was laid out as a shallow V, with its wings stepped back so that every ward had a view of Grand Traverse Bay. Kirkbride put a lot of weight on light, fresh air and pleasant views.

fragments.subject: dumbwaiter
fragments.text: That opening in the wall is a dumbwaiter, a small hand-pulled lift.

fragments.subject: dumbwaiter
fragments.text: In Kirkbride hospitals, meals were cooked in a central kitchen and sent up to each ward's own dining room this way, so patients could eat together on their ward instead of in one huge hall.

fragments.subject: dumbwaiter
fragments.text: There's something resting on the little shelf inside: a bound ledger, by the look of it.

fragments.subject: dining
fragments.text: A ward dining room: a long table and plain wooden chairs, one knocked over.

fragments.subject: dining
fragments.text: Each Kirkbride ward had its own dining room, served from the central kitchen by dumbwaiter. Eating in small groups was meant to feel more like a household than an institution.

fragments.subject: room2
fragments.text: A rusted iron bed frame in a small single room. The window has been boarded over.

fragments.subject: room2
fragments.text: Kirkbride recommended single rooms for most patients, opening off a wide, well-lit corridor. Each one was small, but it was a room of one's own.

fragments.subject: room2
fragments.text: Something green and metal is lying on the floor past the bed: the shade of a desk lamp, by the look of it.

fragments.subject: room4
fragments.text: Another single room, with an iron bed frame and a radiator under the window.

fragments.subject: room4
fragments.text: Kirkbride recommended single rooms for most patients, opening off a wide, well-lit corridor.

fragments.subject: room4
fragments.text: There's a small brass dome on the floor by the radiator. It looks like a desk bell.
